utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the witness, please, Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to tell me how you plan to have these proceedings as cross-examination take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you get the witness, please. No need to wait. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's getting the witness in. But what is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here's my question: I'd like to know how you're going to conduct these proceedings, the cross-examination, because the night before last, which was the earliest possible time that I could do so, because that's when my associate received a binder with the transcripts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let Mr. Lilic take a seat. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, the night before last, which was the time that my associate can visit me at 6.00 p.m., prior to yesterday's day and Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony, I received a binder with the transcripts of some sort of telephone conversations, and that's the binder I have here. And yesterday, when you finished work here and I left, I was given another binder, this one here, with several hundred pages to it of different stenograms with a large number of exhibits, which I also had to read through. And I did manage to read through all this, and of course I can conduct the cross-examination of this witness with respect to the material contained in that binder. However, it's quite obvious that I'm going to need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment. We don't know what this is about. We haven't had these documents, and we don't know what the relevance to this witness is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can deal with -- first of all, the stenographic notes, the stenographic notes of the Council for Coordination, which the Chamber will remember were brought in on the last occasion and have yet to be identified by the witness, the Chamber will recall on the last occasion I said I would go to them probably only for a couple of quotations, and that's my intention in re-examination, because by their late production by the authorities - they have been requested for over a year - it seemed to be quite impossible to have a full examination of the notes by the witness beyond the couple of passages I want him to deal with, one of which he's already dealt with, and the notes will have to speak for themselves. So that is the majority of the documents in the large binder that's been provided to the accused. I wasn't aware that he was being provided with the balance of the documents in that binder. There was no need for him to be provided with those. It's really out of an abundance of generosity, because they are actually documents I may refer to in re-examination. So there was no need to refer him to them now and he's had an advantage that he normally wouldn't otherwise have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that is what that all amounts to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what are you proposing to do this morning? You are going to ask the witness some further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only in -- no, in re-examination. It's all re-examination. If the Court remembers, I left over until today, at the Court's instruction, the question of identification of the stenographic notes, and the other documents are documents that would ordinarily arise in the course of re-examination and have, by one route or another, been provided in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, are they available for us now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They certainly are, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll have them, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My comment and objection had to do with the time that can be given me, because I received the documents just before this session. Regardless of the fact that Mr. Nice just said he's going to skim through them, get through them quickly, I have to ask the witness a number of questions related to those documents. Now, you're giving me one hour, according to Rule 92 bis, whereas I have two large binders here which I was given the night before last and yesterday and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me stop you by saying this: We can -- we can shorten this. In fact, you had half an hour left. But obviously in the light of these new documents, we will consider further time, provided, of course, it's -- it's reasonable. Now, if the Prosecution do not wish to ask any more questions, what we'll do is this: We will go into your cross-examination, you can start asking questions about these documents, we'll see how far we get in half an hour, and then we'll review the position. There's no question, of course, that the original limit would apply if there is new material, which there appears to be. But at the moment, we can't judge precisely how long that time should be. But, of course, we have to bear in mind that the witness has come back especially to continue this evidence and that, therefore, time cannot be endless. But you begin now with your -- your cross-examination. It may be sensible for the witness to have the -- the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, two points: One, I didn't answer one of Your Honour's earlier points. As to the bundle, I repeat that the majority of the documents are intended for re-examination, may or may not be used, and there's no real need for the witness to have them in advance and there's no particular need for the accused to deal with them in advance, but he's simply been provided with them. The other point you asked me about -- or rather, the accused raised and I didn't deal with was transcripts of intercepts. There were some transcripts of intercepts of phone calls with this witness. For example, covering the French airline -- the French pilots and their release, which were provided to the accused out of an abundance of caution and in case they constituted Rule 68 material, and that is why they were provided. So they fall into a different category. But I certainly wouldn't press the witness or the accused to go through the binder of documents at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the difficulty, Mr. Nice, is this: That the more material you supply, the more material you try and use in the case, the more opportunity there is for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And further time. And I think I must ask you to restrict the amount of materials that is now put upon us most carefully, because not only is there the question of time; there's the question of the sheer volume of materials and trying to cope with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All that is very much in my mind. As to the majority of these -- this particular binder, it is, as I say, the stenographic notes. And those are documents that cannot be resisted as documents of value at some stage for consideration but not necessarily with this witness, because of course they -- as the Chamber will recall, they relate to a period of time before he was in office. Indeed, his account is that this particular committee ceased to operate once he came into office. And he gave evidence about simply one passage that he'd read in one of the minutes. There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it would seem sensible if the witness had the binder, in case there are questions to be asked about it. And I see the first tab seems to be 34. Is it proposed it should be additional to the exhibits which we already have for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think 34 is one that I almost certainly won't rely on. It's too substantial and serves a very limited purpose, so I shouldn't trouble too much about that at the moment. But yes, for ease of ordering and recording, they follow along sequentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic, deal if you would with this binder, with those matters on which the witness specifically can deal himself. If there are other matters with which he can't deal, then of course we will allow you to address us on them or to deal with them with some other witness. Yes. Let us begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, don't you think that the fact that Mr. Nice calls additional examination or re-examination in view of these new binders in fact represents the second half time of the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. Let us see how we get on. We've got these documents. The Prosecution say they're going to rely on them. We'll have to see whether they are admissible or not. And what we need to do is to start the examination now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lilic, would you please take a look -- actually, I'm going to start with the binder which relates to the so-called intercepted conversations, the intercepts. And I don't say by chance alleged or so-called because there are things in this material which the term "so-called" -- which merit the term "so-called." Now, Slobodan Milosevic, General Perisic, that particular conversation on the 1st of December, 1995, and the number, Mr. Lilic, is 02263006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The witness doesn't have this bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this? Mr. Kay, can you assist us in this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I really find this amount of material so late confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is Rule 68 material that has been served on the amici and the accused by the Prosecution. It comes as a -- a separate bundle that was delivered to us on the 7th of July, and it is this file that the accused is using to cross-examine the witness with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we copies of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can find some, yes. There's one copy available at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness had better have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have mine, as we can share.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 006, those are the last digits, the last three digits of this ERN number. And it's in the second half of the file of the binder, because the Serbian text is in part 2, 02963006.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine. So the date is the 1st of December, 1995. And for the most part, these conversations relate to the release of the pilots. And I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that "M" is Milosevic and "P" is Perisic. I assume you're able to glean that yourself. Now, I'm just going to refer to a couple of points. "Milosevic: Mladic promised that day when we were in Dobanovci to implement, him, he personally, the investigation to see what had happened to the pilots." Is it true -- do you know that Jacques Chirac called me up in Dayton any number of times to insist that I intervene with respect to the authorities of Republika Srpska to have the pilots found? You remember that, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him asking for that in Dayton. It was even stated that France would place an ultimatum on signing the Dayton Agreement with the release of the pilots, and I do know that he did call for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We insisted, if you remember, on the fact they should give us an answer as to what had happened to the pilots, and they took -- for a long time they said that they had no information about the pilots, that they didn't know what had happened to them; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I say to Perisic, he promised the day we were in Dobanovci that he personally would launch an investigation into the whereabouts of the pilots, because he said he didn't know what had happened to them but he said that he would undertake an investigation to find out. That is what Mladic promised.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what Mladic said, and the others said that they had no knowledge as to the whereabouts of the pilots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I go on to say that it was -- that we had to do this post haste because the conference was coming up and I meant the conference in Paris where the Dayton Agreement was to be signed. And I said, "We have to know their fate in the next day or two." And Perisic says, "I've already called him up and he says he's working on it and he's grumbling and complaining a lot because he's encountering problems." So these two municipality presidents are calling him up. "They have to come and see you. I'll do what I can again," and so on. And I say, "There's no problem there. I will receive them all as of Monday onwards, but I find this question critical because the French are now organising the conference. They are the protagonists of everything. They're friends. And we have to start negotiating with them, and I can't give them an answer as to what happened to the pilots. It's not serious. And quite simply, it devalues everything we've done so far." I'll read a little more slowly. Yes, thank you to the interpreters, because they don't have the text. And then I go on to say, "Please tell him -- let him tell you what he knows straight away and do what he can. I want them found dead or alive. He has to find them." And Perisic says, "Very well." And I once again insist upon this and say that the whole of the public expects it, and we have to be at the conference over there. So the public expects to know." "What do they need those two pilots for? Let them find them." And then I once again say, "He promised, when he was here five days ago --" and I'm referring to Dobanovci. And he said, "I didn't delve into that personally, I couldn't have cared at the time, but I am going to take it into my own hands and do it now personally." So if he is a man of his word, let him see it through. So that, then, is clear, I think, Mr. Lilic, our insistence, I mean, and the clear observation that up until that time the authorities of Republika Srpska had refused to look into any information as to the whereabouts of the pilots. And we insisted that they should be found at all cost. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then turn the page, please. Milutinovic is calling me up, and he says, "I apologise for having to call, but it seems that they're making fools of us collectively." And I say to him the following: "Say what you want." And he says: "Karadzic has stated or, rather, conveyed the message by Daniel Schiffer to Chirac, that man Chirac, that Karadzic would release those two pilots in return for a better status for Republika Srpska." And I say, "You don't say." And Milutinovic says, "Yes. I can't believe that they're saying things like that." And then he goes on to mention some writings of Le Figaro newspaper, and "I'll check it out." And then I say, "Well, check it out and call him. Is it possible that they're taking hostages in that way and making a barter arrangement or blackmail?" And now, our reactions, I say once again, "I can't believe that they're going to be so stupid." And then he says, "Well, we appear to be fools," says Milutinovic towards the end. And I say to him, "We're fools because we want peace." And Milan Milutinovic again says, "Well, quite possibly that he mentioned Schiffer." And I say, "Are you listening to me, Milan? Call him up, because it's impossible that he did something like that. Check it out. And then have them deny it. I don't want -- deny it straight away. Don't shame yourself by doing things like that. Anybody that does things like that, we have nothing to say to him any more and we were resigned because of the statement that reached us," and so on and so forth. The conversation goes on, and I end on the next page and say, "Let them deny this straight away so that they can't blackmail us with these people. It's an ugly thing to do that. This is an opportunity. Fisher gave them the opportunity --" I don't see what I meant there, but anyway, I say, "This is a good opportunity and it's not a good idea for them to blackmail people using human people, human persons." And I say, "Can you explain them to them?" And he says, "Yes, I can." So I insist upon this being done, not only not to complicate matters further but to stick to their word. There's nothing to improve or not improve it. This would be blackmail and the taking of hostages again. Do you remember all that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to those two pilots, I was very well informed. I do remember the efforts that were made to have them released. And you know that I personally took part in their release ultimately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's why I want to go through all this, where your participation is quite obvious. Take a look at the next page, please, 008 are the last three digits of that page, and here is what it says: Slobodan Milosevic talking to an unknown person, and that unknown person you will recognise as being yourself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's me. I've had a chance to look through this. That is me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It says, "Good day, Mr. President. Hello, Mr. President." And I say, "And where are you?" And the answer is, "Here I am in Karadjordjevo." And it said, "I'm sorry, what did you want?" "Well, nothing." And you say, "Well, there's no problem there." I wanted us to meet because you were in Karadjordjevo. And I said, "There's no problem. We won't have much time afterwards. Momir and I are here." And I mean Momir Bulatovic. I wanted to see whether anything could be done, finally, to have those pilots released. Can that man go there and see them for him to show them to him. And if he does that, then this man -- meaning Perisic; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we can say that Perisic has seen them if he does manage to see them, and then the chief of the general staff of France can come over for negotiations, and that's all. And you say, "Well, I can come in the space -- can I come within the hour?" And I say, "Yes, not later than that." And you say, "I'll call Perisic." And I say, "Well, say that matters are hotting up and tell him to go to Mladic, to show him whether he has the pilots or not, because this is an ongoing agony. We haven't had confirmation from him whether he actually has the pilots. If he shows them the pilots, then in the course of the day we'll organise a meeting with the French." And then your answer is, "I'll see to that with him straight away." And when you say "him," you mean Perisic; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if he can tell us that he has the pilots, you say, "So Perisic can be a guarantee, a guarantor that he has the pilots."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I am insisting that you, in view of your function and post, can send Perisic there to establish whether they have the pilots or not. And then Perisic can refer back to us and tell us how things stand. Then I go on to say, "If he believes him, he doesn't have to go, but then he can tell us in writing and sign it that the man has the pilots." And then I go on to say that, "This is the last train out, high time that this were done." And you say, "I'll see to it." And then you continue the conversation on the next page, with the individual -- that is to say, you. You say, "I found Perisic. He believes he can get what you're asking for," and so on. And then I say, "He should tell him that if he's going to bring in the pilots, the man will come to take them over. So he should give guarantees that there won't be any problems on that score." And your answer was, "All right, fine. I've told him to write -- to put it down in writing first." And so on. And you say that you can come to Belgrade. And I say, "Well, don't come to Belgrade before you have the letter, so that we can see what the letter says." And then you go on to explain that you're there with your wife, and I say, "My best regards to your wife." And that's all. And now you have on that same page a conversation between you and Perisic, in which you explain the problem to him. His response was, "I can guarantee that to you." And then, "To hell with what happens to me but that our state guarantees for somebody else's risky business." So does that show that Perisic isn't sure he has the pilots?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that point in time, I don't think anybody knew where the pilots were on our side. Their side, of course, did know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not even Perisic knew. And you say to him, "They accept everything Momo asked for and Perisic asked "everything?" And you say, "Everything he asked for. They guarantee everything." And Perisic says, "Yes." And then again you say the following: "Let him write it down. Let him put in writing that they have him. Let him come to talk and negotiate and hand the people over," and so on. And then you go on to say, "We'll call the French only once he confirms that they have them. Otherwise, there's no point." And then you threaten them and say that "If they fail to comply, they will have to bear the consequences."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why is this being -- what has this been disclosed at this stage in the proceedings? I don't -- I simply don't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution and on the possibility of it being 68 as against this witness, showing his measure of control. And that is all. It's outside the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why wasn't it disclosed earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where a decision is changed or where a decision is modulated, one has to act accordingly. But the witness is capable of giving a summary account of all this. And any point that the accused wants to be put can be put summary. And there's one point that I will want to raise in re-examination. That's all. But we also only got it very recently, as a matter of fact, from sources that provided it. But it has very limited value. Nevertheless, we have to be so careful with our 68 obligations that if in doubt, we provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, will you take this as expeditiously as you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very expeditious with these transcripts. But I have to say that Mr. Nice's explanation absolutely is not convincing, that this can be harmful to the witness, because the role of the witness in this is a highly positive one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He didn't say -- he did not say it would be harmful to the witness. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be more expeditious, I will skip over to page 13. "Milosevic, with an unknown person, X," I assume --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's quite obvious. You say, "Mr. President, this is how things stand. I'm chasing this idiot. He was in Sarajevo. From Sarajevo he went to Kalinovik, from Kalinovik to Srbinje. Anyway, he's walking around the hills," et cetera. And then you say, "Perisic is suggesting two things. I don't know why that we go there together to persuade him with regard to the pilots. That is one possibility. And the other is for him to go there alone." And I reply, "Let him go alone, but let him see whether he has the pilots." You've found that place, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even Perisic can still not guarantee that they have the pilots. Then I say, "Well, who can provide guarantees?" And you say, "Perisic." And I say, "Let him write that down." And then you tell me what he told you, that he can't do that in relation to another state but he can provide us guarantees. And I say, "Well, let them provide us with guarantees. Let him write down for you that he has them and that this one will bring them over. And then we'll bring the chief of staff of France for this to be over tomorrow." "Very well, Mr. President." So that is it, as far as that intercept is concerned. Then he's conditioning things. This is page 14. And you are talking to Perisic, asking, "Is my word and your word and Chirac's word and Slobodan's word, are they enough for him," as obviously he's doubtful. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you make arrangements for going there together, and that's on page 15. I won't dwell on that any further. And just let me draw attention to page 16. Again, a transcript of a conversation between Mr. Milosevic and an unknown person, and that is you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only it keeps says "president of the assembly." There are many errors in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, there are many errors. But the gist of the conversation is there. And then you say, "Fine. I'll go there if you say so. There's no question about it." And then you say that "He should come with us to have guarantees that what we have proposed is for sure, that he has them over there. He doesn't have them 60, he has two of them." And I'm asking again, "Well, will he bring them?" "No, he wants to talk to them and then he says he'll come to Belgrade." And I say, "Well, let him come to Belgrade, but you see those men first. You make sure you see them." And you say, "So we should see them." And then several lines later, "And convince him to bring them so that they can be near at hand for him to be able to hand them over." And then you say, "He claims 100 per cent that he has them. We've talked three times just now." And I say, "Yes, it is important for him to say whether he has them or not and for Perisic to say that he has them." And then you reply, "He says he has them 100 per cent. We spoke three times, and he says that the only problem is the Tribunal, that he promised him that and then what happens?" My answer is, "Nothing. Tell him we promise him that we will not surrender him." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, we didn't surrender anyone to this illegal Tribunal anyway. "And give us the men." The reference is to the pilots. And then you say "let me -- should I give him my word?" I say, "Write it down, that we will not surrender him to the Tribunal if he surrenders the pilots," and you say, "Fine." "And don't let him come here, but let him give you the pilots," et cetera. To save time, I won't go into any details. These are marathon-like conversations between you and Perisic regarding guarantees. Mention is made of Slobodan and Chirac, et cetera, et cetera. I won't dwell on this any longer now. On page 25, or rather, 030 are the last digits, we make arrangements for Perisic to host his French counterpart and remind him once again, I say that, "This man cannot go back without taking those men with him." And then again, on page 31, a conversation between Perisic and Lilic. You say, "I've passed on to Slobodan the main points. I didn't say what the special terms are so as not to cause problems right out. What is important for me, and I think you agree, is that this chief of staff come tomorrow," and the reference is to the chief of staff of the French general staff. And then, after that, you did go to Republika Srpska, together with Perisic. I cautioned you that they shouldn't show you any idiots. And your answer is, "Well, surely they must speak the language of the country they come from so that they don't cheat you." Isn't that right? And all the whole story ended fortunately, had a happy ending. The pilots were released, and we can see from this that no one among the people in Yugoslavia until the very last moment knew whether those men were in their hands, whether they were alive at all, whether they could be handed over, et cetera. In your opinion, was it possible to invest more effort than we did to ensure the success of this operation and for the pilots to be found?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that I was personally involved in this, and at one point you were against my involvement. You said that it would be better for Perisic to go alone. But then we decided that I should go after all. I think that I never had a more difficult task in my life than to save those two pilots, in view of the overall behaviour of the entire main staff, not General Ratko Mladic, who were concealing their whereabouts. And I think that the intelligence administration of the Army of Yugoslavia did everything possible and used all possible channels to find them, and they couldn't, until General Ratko Mladic himself said that he was holding them at Han Pijesak, and even then he didn't want to show them, he just promised to hand them over. I could describe in detail the whole event and the conditions he set and all the things he demanded in return for the pilots. And among other things, that the whole Supreme Council should sign this document. This happened during the night. I know I came to see you at 1.00 a.m. In any event, I think that as far as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is concerned, an enormous effort was invested to save those pilots in the first place, to save their lives, and that the chief of staff of the French army - I think his name was Jean Douin - himself caused some problems when talking to Ratko Mladic. He didn't want to talk to a man who was on the list of suspected war criminals. But when all is said and done, I think that it ended happily, and I think that it was a good move prior to the signing of the agreement in Paris. What is also interesting, with regard to those pilots is that I think it was the 11th of December when Radovan Karadzic himself called up and he wanted to get the Russian intelligence service involved in this, and I warned Perisic to take care that they don't spoil the whole arrangement made with Ratko Mladic in that way. The pilots were handed over to General Douin at the bridge at Zvornik safe and sound, and I think they had even been operated on in the hospital in Han Pijesak in Republika Srpska. That would be the story in very brief. So it was thanks primarily to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that this was achieved. I did sign that famous paper on which Ratko Mladic insisted that he shouldn't be surrendered to The Hague Tribunal, referring and relying to our constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely so. And that is not at all at issue. That was our position throughout and continues to be my position today. Now, will you please help me. Will you turn the page, 039. It doesn't relate to you, but it does relate to a phenomenon illustrating the kinds of things that can be found in transcripts of this kind. And what is the purpose of planting such documents. 039.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the audiotape of this conversation to be played so that Mr. Lilic and those listening can see that this allegedly is a conversation between my wife and Rajko Banduk, Mladic's secretary, a low-ranking officer, in which she asks him to explain, and at the very beginning TV France is saying something in three parts. Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with this. First of all, I need to be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pointed to the position in this transcript. Where in the English is this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's 11/12/95 is the date on the intercept, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11th of December, 1995. Mr. May, this is just a drop in the sea of untruths that are being published daily against me and my wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't -- don't make speeches at this stage. Now, what is the point that you want to make with this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to prove that this is a complete falsehood, because my wife never spoke to some sort of secretary of Mladic, asking him whether the pilots were alive. Just imagine. It says -- she talks to Rajko as if they were on good terms. And said, "I don't want to be an obstacle to President Milosevic. And we spent our whole life together" and she says that she doesn't want to stand in my way." A whole lot of nonsense. I'd like the sound to be played. Because Mr. Lilic knows my wife and her voice, and this absolutely cannot be her. This is not just a drop in the ocean of lies published daily against me but also as evidence that false documents are being produced here, unverified documents. This is not the yellow press; it should be least one step above.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness can identify the voice. Mr. Lilic, do you think you can identify the accused's wife's voice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if we can get it played.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not even sure we have the actual audiotapes. We have the transcripts. These have not been produced by us. They've been provided to the accused under Rule 68 as material coming into our possession. We know that the witness confirms the accuracy of the transcripts that he's reviewed, but there's no part of our case that the other material is going in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, no doubt you'll see if you could find the tapes, if that's been put in evidence. We haven't got the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, please look at the transcript itself. Look at the end of the page, please. "I don't wish to be an obstacle to President Milosevic." It's not -- I'm not saying that this is a suspicious conversation. This person is enquiring into the life of the pilots. But this is a fabrication simply that my wife would communicate at all with the secretary of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can answer -- you've made your point. The witness can answer as far as he can. Mr. Lilic, do you know anything at all about this? You've heard what the accused is -- is putting. Can you say whether -- can you add anything to it? That's his account. Do you know if Mrs. Markovic was in touch with this man? Can you help either way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether she was in touch with him, Mr. May. But if I may, I have read through these transcripts. I said of some of them that they certainly correspond to the time and events I was involved in at the time, but I must admit that I was sincerely astonished when I read this text that Mr. Milosevic is referring to and also the method of communication with Warrant Officer Banduk, surprised by any direct link between them and surprised by the contents of this text, because the day before that I was in Bosnia. I was in Han Pijesak on the 10th of December. So my astonishment was extreme when I saw this, and I said that I wasn't sure that this was possible. If it's possible, then it indicates quite different relationships that I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is anything like this possible at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not sure, especially this last conversation where you're calling from your daughter's on a private telephone, talking about such things. I don't know. I must be quite frank. This was -- I was astonished by this text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this woman says, "I'm calling from my daughter's apartment." It's absolute nonsense, this. Isn't that clear, at least?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text appears to show that Mrs. Markovic has extremely good relations with Ratko and Tolimir, which was not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She didn't even know who Tolimir was, nor the generals that are mentioned there, and you know that very well. But I would like to tape to be played for the witness to be able to hear it, and I would like to hear it too. It's really disgraceful that something like this should be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got any more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must repeat: This isn't being tendered as evidence. It's being produced by the accused because material of this kind has to be produced by us to him for him to use. But if he doesn't believe there's any truth in it, then it's a waste of time for him to refer to it, because I'm not going to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They're not going to rely on this in evidence. Now, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now we come to the last conversation from these transcripts, which I would like you to comment on. The page is 042. It says: "Slobodan Milosevic calling from Karadjordjevo with Ljubica, Zoran Lilic, and General Momcilo Perisic, or rather, the other way round. You were in Karadjordjevo with your wife and Perisic and I'm talking to you and Perisic; right? But it doesn't matter. That's just a technical point. First, a few sentences -- I exchange a few words with your wife. I wish her bon voyage, because you were off to China and so on. And then she sends her regards to my wife and she says, "Here's Zoran for you. Goodbye." Milosevic says, "Hello, Zoki." Lilic says, "Here I am with Momcilo and we're discussing something," and Milosevic says, "That's very good. It would be a good idea for him to contact these friends of his because it would be an important thing" - and bear in mind that this is the 16th of December, 1995 - "it would be important for them to assume a positive position at the assembly, not with respect to the plan. They have to accept the plan. That is not the problem. And they have accepted it. They have accepted it. But they must realise that the most important thing now is to have good relations with IFOR, to have good relations with these peace forces." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the agreement was accepted. We discussed it in the previous conversation when we were discussing Dayton. And then I go on to say the following: "The only question is: Are they going to confirm the thing that they are allies with the Americans or are they going to leave that to the Muslims? We have traditional relationships of alliance with the Americans," and so on and so forth. And then I say, "bon voyage," and then I ask to speak to Perisic, who spoke to me in your presence. And then I say the same thing to him, "It would be a good idea if you were to hear -- contact those people of yours across the Drina." And he says, "Yes." "With respect to the assembly." There's just one question, as the plan is no longer contested. There's just one outstanding question that is important for them. Are they going to show from the very beginning that we are in an alliance with the Americans, or is that alliance going to be left to the Muslims?" And Perisic says, "Yes, I understand." We always had traditional allied relationships with them. The Muslims were always at war with them. So now is the best time to assert the traditional alliance and not leave it to the Muslims. And I think that somebody should represent -- should do something along those lines and to represent their army before the assembly and speak. So you suggest that to them, please. You put it to them, please." And then I say again, "What I told you, that Clinton told me in Paris that those Mujahedins would slit his throat first and then the throats of all the Americans." And then I sad, "So the Serb side is expected to behave towards them as towards friends and allies, and they must be able to demonstrate that from day one. That is the basic point. Everything else has been solved. I just don't want them to be led astray by that man over there with all his nonsenses. That's the only important thing." And then I state again, "Let's see how things will evolve today, because there might be individuals over there. And I ask you that your service take this into account. I say this to Perisic, and see how people are acting, because anybody working against --" and we mean the mission and the implementation of the Dayton Accords -- "anybody working against that," I say, "against the interests of the people and peace, we're going to arrest them all. So do that, please, so we know who is on whose side. See to it." And then I repeat at the end, I say to him, "It's important that the army at the assembly should state this. We were always traditional allies. America is there and we want those relations to be placed in the best possible status urgently. So relations and cooperation are the number-one priority." Do you remember that conversation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you also remember that we endeavoured at all events that after the Dayton Agreements were signed, that we were to -- we wielded all our influence to prevent a single incident from breaking out. And in actual fact, no incidents did come to pass. Now, I'd like to go on to the next tab -- or rather, not tab but binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal first of all with these tapes. Do you want them exhibited, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I do, Mr. May, because they indicate quite clearly not only goodwill and maximum efforts on our part but that good faith should be -- should prevail in all these undertakings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, first of all, thank you for the loan. I think I'll return it. Is there any reason why we shouldn't exhibit them? It would seem sensible to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Defence rely on it. It shows -- it shows criticism of the RS leadership, that they weren't working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's crucial to the accused's case, and it's plainly material that has been introduced through this witness that he's correctly identified in the terms that the accused has put to him, and thereby adopted the material. And plainly it would be admissible. This witness was very much involved with those events that we're dealing with and was able to speak of the accuracy of the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll get an exhibit number for them, and then I want to raise something about the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They're transcripts, of course, at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The transcripts of tapes, not the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, rather than tapes. We have to wait the originals, if they are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They will be exhibited, and no doubt copies can be made available for the Bench. The next matter I want to raise is the status of this binder, which I do not understand why this is arriving now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it was a mistake. I wasn't intended to be provided now. It's a sort of bit of good fortune for the accused. That is the exhibits that I would have taken Lilic to -- Mr. Lilic to in re-examination in certain circumstances, almost certainly. It also includes the stenographic notes of the meeting of the Council for Coordination, and those have got to be dealt with because those are left over from last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They -- is that right, that they had not been provided at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me remind you of the history: Shortly before the last hearing, there was a concluded 54 bis application with some decisions. These minutes were not the subject of an order, and to our surprise and pleasure they were provided voluntarily on, I think, the morning of the first day that Mr. Lilic gave evidence, is my recollection, something like that. We heard about it, and we were able to produce them because they were flown up specially on the day that he last gave evidence on the last occasion. And I had announced that it might be thought convenient simply for him to identify them so that they could be then processed as an identified exhibit. In the event, we ran out of time and the Court thought it better to put back their identification until a later stage. And so that is an independent exercise that needs to be done at some stage today, and that relates to the largest physical part of this binder. Those documents have yet to be translated in full, and I have simply two extracts from them translated that I want to raise with the witness at some stage, one that he's already dealt with in evidence from memory. So that accounts for a number of these exhibits, and the number that it relates to is in this particular bundle, it's numbers 39 and 40, 41, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What it -- the remaining documents, have they been exhibited to date, or are you seeking now to put them in?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. They're documents that I would be coming to in re-examination. Some of them are new documents that have simply arrived since Mr. Lilic gave evidence, a couple of them, and the others are documents that, in light of the answers he gives, I wish to put to him along with one or two other exhibits already produced. Obviously, typically he would not have seen these in advance of the conclusion of his cross-examination and nor would the accused, so that they come to the accused in a sense by way of the accused's good fortune. But the appropriate course would be for him to conclude his cross-examination in lines with his earlier plan, and for the matter to unfold in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Except that would mean he wouldn't be able to cross-examine about the new documents you're putting in. So I think it's better today --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I can identify those to him in any event, because they weren't available to him before. Let me just find their numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll allow the cross-examination to continue. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. New -- I'm very concerned about new material coming in in re-examination, because it makes it very difficult for the accused to respond in any effective form to it. And it may have -- the evidence itself may have a completely different perspective from his position. We've seen that in a number of cases with documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 37 and 38 are the documents that are -- are simply not available before, but I think - and I'll check this - I think that's the only two that are other than previously available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAY
utterances.text: I think it's right that the accused should have the opportunity to cross-examine on the entire binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I see you -- your headsets weren't on. I demand for reasons of principle that the tape of the alleged conversation between my wife and that warrant officer, where she's asking whether the pilots are alive, should be placed for expert analysis to see whether the voice is hers. You have examples of her voice in interviews and in other things. Because I don't think forgeries of this kind ought to be allowed by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have the tape. I've made it plain twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with it in this way and explain the position: The tape is not available. The Prosecution do not have it. We will see if it can be obtained. But you should also understand this, that the Prosecution are not putting this forward as part of their case. It's merely part -- documents that they've disclosed to you. Somebody has passed it to them and they've passed it on to you. They're not going to rely on it. Now, if it becomes relevant, we will try and pursue the matter. But for the moment, it is not evidence at all in the case. So whatever its background, it doesn't really matter. Now, let's -- let's move on, because time is -- is limited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm not speaking about the context. The context is positive. She's interested about the lives of the pilots and she speaks about the French interest. But I'm speaking about maliciousness and that a contact of some kind is indicated. And it is relevant because it's just a drop in the ocean of lies that are being put out every day precisely against my wife, myself, and my family. So it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The relevance here is what is evidence in this particular case, and that is what we're concerned with. Now, let's move on. You can ask questions now about this binder. Does the witness have the binder? He has it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I do hope that you have the file too and that you can see that it numbers several hundred pages and was disclosed to me last night -- or rather, yesterday, once you had left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, first of all, let's just take a look at this. They are stenographic notes from the extended meeting of the Council for dovetailing positions of state policy. It was formed and presided over by the then-president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a highly respected personage, the greatest living Serb writer. He is the senior of us all. He is the eldest. And his desire was to collect together the representatives of Serbia, Montenegro, Krajina, Republika Srpska, to hold consultations about political issues; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to the best of all intentions, to set a unified political approach to questions and issues having to do with Serb national interests; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that can be clearly seen from the stenographic notes themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it then clear that the intention was a constructive one on the part of Mr. Cosic and in all respects a good one? And judging by what we're going to go through now, it is obvious that it is oriented towards peace; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this council was never a secret. It was -- it made public for the information media individual positions taken by it, of course, once they had been decided, and it was -- the decision to set it up in the first place was made public too. It was public knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just speaking of this good intention and the efforts made of the then-president of the FRY to gather together the leadership and in the function of peaceful solutions and the best possible solutions to hold consultations of this kind. Isn't that right? Now, in these stenographic notes, we have several interventions on my part recorded, and I notice that Mr. Nice has highlighted just one, one of those several interventions. However, the comprehensive nature of the efforts made at that meeting would be distorted were we not to take a look at at least some of the many interventions made at the meeting. And now please turn to page 39. I don't want to give you the ERN number because the stenographic notes are paginated, so it is on page 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which tab? Which tab is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably 40, because he's starting there. There are no translations of these. They are not ready yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It is tab 39. It is the meeting of the 21st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist you? It was the 9th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have it as being the 21st of January, 1993. They're the stenographic notes from the expanded session, 21st of January, 1993, and the number is 02944123.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have 3994 as the last digits on my page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it's another number and another document. I don't have the 9th of January document, I fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got -- Mr. Lilic, it's tab 39. Perhaps if someone would just assist the witness with the tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, it is tab 40 is the one of the 9th of January, according to my binder. So maybe under tab 40 Mr. Lilic has what is tab 39 in the other binder. So we're talking about these two tabs, 39 and 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness look at tab 39. Look at 39.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it, the 21st of January. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, before we consider this page or these pages that I should like to comment on briefly and quote from, I have noticed - and maybe you have the same document - that out of the whole minutes, only one insert has been chosen in English, and it comes before the Serbian stenographic notes. And this abstract is a quotation of Zivota Panic, General Zivota Panic. I assume that Mr. Nice did this to ask you about that, so I will take the opportunity to put a question to you about it because afterwards they won't let me have the floor. What has been translated into English is to be found in the Serbian language on page 34 of the original stenographic notes. Have you found it, I assume?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will not analyse the entire text. It begins with Dobrica Cosic asking, "Who wants the floor? I give the floor to General Panic." Then it says, "Zivota Panic," and he speaks. And then on page 34, in the central large paragraph, he explains that the situation is very bad. He addresses himself to Cosic, saying, "What is happening on the left bank of the Drina around Srebrenica, Bajina Basta, Bratunac, is so bad, and you, Mr. President, should know that it's a disgrace for the Serbian people. They're fleeing. They're abandoning everything. The aid we are giving them in weapons, ammunition is in certain houses in the village. We were not able to pull it out. We are preparing to destroy it. That is what was left behind by the JNA." And it is the following that I wish to ask you to comment on, because he says, "In personnel, the army -- in terms of personnel, the army should not go to alien territory but volunteers should be found, some men who will save that part of the territory," and so on. So my question is: Is it clear that since the founding of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and after the withdrawal of the JNA and the formation of the Army of Yugoslavia, there were no units of the Army of Yugoslavia that could be sent to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Because he himself says, "We cannot send personnel to foreign territory." So the question is: Is it true that whether we're talking of the Republic of Serbia or the Republic of Montenegro, either, that only volunteers went to Bosnia and Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke at some length about this during the previous hearing, and I even underlined that after 1992 not a single armed unit of the Army of Yugoslavia was located in the territory of the Republic of Srpska upon orders of the Supreme Defence Council. And this also applies to the period when Mr. Cosic was president. Not then and not throughout your term of four years. And your term of office ended on the 25th of June, 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is two years after the Dayton Agreement and the cessation of the war; is that right? So you're able to testify about the entire period. Now, please look at page 39. Is this, too, the principled position that I advocated within our leadership in the republic and which I hope you are very familiar with? I'm asking for the floor. This is on page 39. And I say, "I suggest that we try to see in concrete terms what awaits us in Geneva." We are discussing the conference in Geneva. And I say that "Momir and Sveta are right." And I'm referring to Momir Bulatovic and Sveta Stojanovic. That is also my opinion. "Our position is that of a principled participant who is advocating a peaceful settlement to the crisis, and we have done our utmost for a principled platform to be defined." Isn't that right? Isn't that our position throughout, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I say, I quote: "Our attitude, that is, that of the delegation of Yugoslavia, is quite different with regards to maps, military agreements, and other specific questions, which on the basis of the principles that we have advocated truly belong to issues that the three parties should negotiate." I mean the Muslim, the Serbian, and Croat, within Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. I quote again: "Our position should be one of principle, in favour of peace and a consensus among the three parties for an equitable protection, an even-handed protection of the interests of all three nations." Is that what it says, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with my position which I underlined frequently and emphasised that peace in Bosnia would be achieved once the interests of all three nations are treated even-handedly? Wasn't that my position from the very outset?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. And that was repeated umpteen times, not your thesis, but your principled position. Before you continue with your questions, Mr. May, if I may, I would like to inform you and the Trial Chamber with the following: I did see four out of seven of these stenographic notes in 1993 to inform myself with them to the extent that this was necessary in view of the position I took as president of FRY. I was not a participant in all these meetings that were held. I can only analyse them from the position of my knowledge and familiarity with the political situation but not as a participant. So please appreciate that position, if I'm not very precise about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll -- we'll bear that in mind. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But surely you consider yourself quite qualified to assess the political nature and content of certain quotations.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was the policy that I advocated, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at the next paragraph: "Therefore, we support all the three parties, and that they should sit round the table and agree on specific matters, maps, other military, and other matters. That is the principled position of our delegation, which means that we support all three parties and their mutual agreement. Whatever that may be, we will support it." Isn't that right? And then I go on to say that "We should not interfere into what the three parties should negotiate." On the next page, second paragraph, I say, "I spoke to Vance today and he asked me directly 'what do you think the approach to maps should be?' I told him quite frankly that the maps should be approach with a great deal of patience and as a highly delicate matter and that maps were factual matters." And then I mentioned the 1991 census. I say that "We have the 1981 map, and the principle should be that territory taken by force should not be accepted and existing maps indicate what belongs to whom regarding the borders of the provinces." This is all part of the Vance-Owen Plan, when they organised and drew up provinces that were to be set up in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have the censuses. You have everything. We shouldn't -- I don't say that we do not accept but that territory taken by force should not be recognised and that things should be solved in a principled manner. Then I go to point out -- and this is on page 42. I will skip over things. I say in the third paragraph, fourth line from the top, Since there is reference there to the entire Geneva package, including military matters, I say, "I am not a military expert and I don't see -- I don't know what is very important and what is not. We have a principled position, and that is there can be no one-sided disarming. That principled position is something we can defend with a clear conscience." And then I repeat again: "We must respect the principle that territory taken by force cannot be acknowledged, but this applies far more to the Croats than to the Serbs," et cetera. And then I say, "If a military agreement is agreed upon, we've taken an enormous step forward for the shootings to stop and for these things to be done by political means." And then there's a comment as to who is for peace and who is for war. So is it quite clear what, as a matter of principle, Serbia, and I personally as the president of Serbia, were advocating at that Council for Coordination of Positions that was being held with the highest representatives listed present? Will you now look at page 47, please. When I intervene, after it is said that it is contradictory for problems to be solved quickly, I say, "It is in contradiction with the situation. It is normal and logical for them to push the military document in the interest of a cessation of the conflict." So I am saying that it is -- that we should accept as normal their insistence of the military document because it is in the interest of the cessation of hostilities, as soon as possible. And then I cannot remember - and will you please remind me --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't seem to be getting to a question. And can I raise now, just before we break, the general approach the Chamber, and we, and the accused, and the amici may be obliged to take in relation to records of this type. I've referred to it before, and I think the use of this type of record has got to be seen in the history of the production of the records to us and the problems that that has created. But immediately, there doesn't seem to be a question. It just seems to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm allowing him to read. If he wants to read into the record, he can. He's entitled to rely on this. Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. May. You have surprised me pleasantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, Vladimir Vojvodic should be a general; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because I know Vladimir Vojvodic who was the head of the military medical academy. I can't remember this one. Was -- what was he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is the one, actually. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the doctor? Oh, it could be.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I think he was in Mr. Cosic's team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Quite. Perhaps. Now, let's see. He explains on page 51: "Vladimir, Vojvodic, he says, that must be done, because that is a precondition. That is what it says, an agreement on peace. That is the heading." And then Ilija Djukic takes the floor. Ilija Djukic at the time was the Minister for Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Vlado, but they intimated they would seek a complete cease-fire at midnight Saturday." Vladimir Vojvodic says, "That is something new." Then Slobodan Milosevic, "That should be accepted immediately. It's something that we should even propose, Saturday, midnight, a complete cessation of fire, and we should abide by it and respect it." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Karadzic: "No, it's better for them to propose because if we make the proposal then they call into question the second part of the plan. It's better to put it forward at private meetings and with friends." And I say, "Yes, but we should accept straight away a complete cessation of hostilities on Saturday midnight." Is it possible to insist in more categorical terms than this, "accept immediately what they are suggesting, midnight Saturday? They said something new and I react by saying, "It should be accepted immediately. It should even be our proposal, a complete cessation of fire on Saturday midnight and we should respect it."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try and finish this. Again on page 54, Slobodan Milosevic: "As there's a great deal of discussion about this, the Assembly of Republika Srpska at Pale has taken a favourable position, and I say, "Let's be specific. Last time a paper of 9 points was put on the table. I believe that that piece of paper with nine points will be verified." And then the next sentence is, "The reply of the Serbian side is yes, because the decision of the assembly is yes." Before that, there are comments about it, but I'm saying that the answer is yes. "It will be a trick that I believe will be resorted to, and that is the question will be asked whether the Serb side has any reservations in that connection," et cetera, "in order to detract from the value of the positive outcome of the Assembly meeting at Pale, because some parties will insist on that, not Vance and Owen, but they will intervene with them to that effect. The answer should be no tricks and no reservations. This nine-point document has been accepted. Therefore, we have opened the way to discussions on other matters; maps, a military agreement, et cetera, so we shouldn't fall into the trap of admitting that there were any kind of reserves there, that we are saying, 'Yes, but.' It is not 'Yes, but.' It is not 'Yes, but.' It is 'Yes.' In response to the paper, the document put on the table in Geneva at our plenary meeting that we held on Tuesday. And if they'd note that in plenary --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must bring this to a close now. It's time for an adjournment. Mr. Nice, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to explain what I was going to propose as a way of dealing with this type of record. Self-evidently we've always wanted this material to be available to the Court, because if it's the precise words of the accused, then it's really the best evidence of what he was thinking and saying at the time. That is why we've pursued these documents since we first learnt of their existence from this witness. We've managed to produce for you the Dobanovci documents, which were tab 20 of the Lilic exhibit, and we're still hoping to get for you the rather larger volume of material from the Supreme Defence Council minutes, at which this witness indeed was a chairman and participant. We know there's a -- perhaps a short delay, but they aren't yet with us, and the Chamber will also recall that the witness was not inclined to deal with even the meetings at which he'd been a participant without having a full record before him. But if we get all those documents before you in due course, then there will be a long record of what the accused said in meetings of this kind. Now, it seemed to me that with that quantity of material coming late, through no fault of ours, because we've been trying to get hold of it one way or another for nearly two years, the better course would probably be for all of us to read the material once it's in translation outside court, if that is a possibility, thus to restrict cross-examination on the material to what -- to that which can be conveniently accommodated within the limited time available to us. Because otherwise -- and I'm not, of course, standing in the way of the material going in; to the contrary, I want it all to go in. And I of course know in general terms what this amounts to, although it isn't available in cross-examination. To allow it to be read in, if it becomes the practice, will be enormously time consuming. So I made some reference to this on the last occasion when I expressed the hope the documents would in due course, as it were, speak for themselves or be capable of being read rather than being read into the record. And that is something I would urge the Chamber to consider because of the real problems of time. Fundamentally, I stick by the position that if this is - I have no reason to doubt it - the precise words of the accused in various meetings, it's obviously valuable material. The question is simply how to handle it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is the fair way in which the deal with it. How long is this witness here for?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, he's only here for today. I don't know about his availability for tomorrow. But, Your Honour, I mean, thinking, as it were, ahead or back, had we had the material earlier, we might have been able to schedule it and present it through a witness or an expert. But it simply hasn't -- hasn't arrived until now. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the position and we'll consider the time which should be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I realise you've already ruled against me on this, but it would be my submission that for a witness who has said he's not even prepared to deal with the meetings where he was a participant, say, with a record, there must be a limited value to the answers he can give on meetings at which he wasn't present. The Chamber will recall that he, apart from the one extract we've looked at in part, which was translated, he -- he was struck by one other entry, which we can see at the beginning of tab 40. He gave an account of that. And this is the -- as it were, the full and corrected version of that. And those are the only two excerpts I'd be relying on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to balance the various interests in this case in deciding how to progress from here. We have in mind what the Prosecution said about time, of course. At the same time, the accused must be entitled, faced with this vast volume of documents, to make use of them and to cross-examine upon them, on matters he considers relevant. But we also have to take account the interests of the witness who has returned to give evidence, here to assist the Court, who now also finds himself confronted with a battery of documents, his having agreed to come back for an hour and a half. As against that, we have the general interests of justice. We've come to this conclusion: Having regard to the matter which the accused has to deal with today and having regard to the fact that the amici, I think, asked for half an hour and the Prosecution half an hour, we shall give them the last session to share between them. This next session we will allow for cross-examination, which means the accused will have had over two and a half hours this morning, which we deem to be sufficient. So, Mr. Milosevic, you've got the next session, if you want it, if you require it, to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So a shortened session, Mr. May. But nonetheless, I'll do my best to get through my main points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And not to lose time, let me start, Mr. Lilic. Would you please open tab 4 -- no, 40, I'm sorry, tab 40, which is also -- which is also the stenographic notes from an extended session for the council on the dovetailing of positions on state policy, dated the 9th of January, 1993, the Council for Coordination. And as you've taken a look at both these stenographic notes, they actually make up a whole, don't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with the first stenographic notes, Mr. Nice highlighted a portion and had it translated in English, the one we discussed with Zivota Panic and his statement. And we explained that nobody from the army could go across the Drina River. Now, with these second lot of minutes, which is -- makes up a whole with the first part, he highlighted another portion, that is to say, a short intervention by me, and had it translated into English, but we'll come to that later on, when the time comes, according to the order of things. There were quite a number of interventions from my part, on my part, and this one instance in the context of all the others is a very good one too. Now, take a look, please, at the stenographic notes. I'll try and get through them as quickly as possible. But look at page 34, please. Page 34, the penultimate paragraph. And I'm going to start off by reading out the third sentence. We're all speaking round the table, and I assume we all share each other's opinions, and then I go on to quote what I said at the time. "It is our strategic goal that the Serb people in the Balkans should be free and equal.
