Freedom and equality for the Serb people in the Balkans implies each and every possibility for it to assert fully and realise its interests." And then I go on to conclude at the end of that paragraph, "For me it is less important through harmony, institutional solutions, and stages that goal is to be reached, and what is much more important for me is how many people are going to die for those goals and whether anybody ought to lay down their lives at all for any of those goals." So was that always our position? We are not seeking anything more than equality. We want to be equal and free. Isn't that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Many of us took the same position that you put forward here, and those were our positions of principle and publicly declared positions. So that's not just something that happened at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm sure you'll remember when the declaration of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established and when the constitution was enacted the declaration was registered in the United Nations as an official document of our country, by the way, and it stated that "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has no territorial pretensions vis-a-vis the former Yugoslav republics." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the document when the new constitution was enacted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm sure you'll also remember that I stated publicly at the assembly in Pale, I stressed the goal, the objective which was freedom and equality and not -- nothing more than that, and of course nothing less than that. And then, take a look at page 35, the next page. I say that "Nobody should lose their lives, regardless of the institutional phases and stages necessary for the negotiations, that one should be persistent in negotiating." And then I go on to conclude, at the top of the page, that "Even one single head less for the realisation of goals, which means if even one man is killed, that is always more than a phase, inter-phase, step, inter-step, in an institutional solution on negotiations being conducted." So what I am saying is that we must insist on negotiations and a peaceful solution regardless of how long those negotiations will last and how many negotiations we have to go through. Was that our position and policy, the policy we pursued?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now take a look at page 36, please, where I state the following: I mention the talks with Cyrus Vance and the formula, in inverted commas, because this is taken over from a document prepared by them, "Three constituent nations, peoples." And then we say that "That formula must be asserted in the ten principles, three constituent nations, peoples." And I say - and then he said - "All right. Very well. Let's do it this way. Let's have the first principle read that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a decentralised state composed of three constituent peoples and organised into provinces with a high degree of the exercise of power and authority." So that is what the international mediators agreed to. That was our goal, and that was a function of the fact that the Serb people should be free and equal, never to the detriment of the other two peoples. Was that always our policy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in this case, I think it was -- it referred to a preparation of that future, the future constitution should the Vance-Owen Plan be realised. So this term "constituent peoples" is a very important one, "three constituent peoples."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of page 36 there, the last sentence, "If you go with the principle of three constituent peoples and their equality, then I assume those three peoples must arrive at the definition of their constitution." So we strove to have these three constituent peoples define their constitution together themselves. And then, I'm sure you'll remember, this was another topic of our discussions. I think that after Dayton you signed this with the representatives of Republika Srpska, that is to say, the agreement, special relations or --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, special relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a topical issue. So I say -- another question that I broached was the decisive exclusion of coming into relationship with others, which Vance took in fairly well and said that that question wasn't to be raised, to enter into a relationship with others, that that could be relativised and improved. So is it clear that we accept -- we were ready to accept any solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina which showed a respect for the equality of the constituent nations and it implied that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a single state?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the three sides were to reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And that with full conscience is the only proper course and principle to take. I hope you'll agree with that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now take a look at page 50, because this also relates to this -- these relationships. Once again, "Slobodan Milosevic: Regional institutions are not excluded at all and I broached the question with Vance." And then I go on to say, "With Serbia, for example. Within the of the former Yugoslavia we had relations with the Northern Rhine area, for example, that is the Westfalia German province of the North Rhine or with an Italian province, for example." As there, we had the Heilongjiang province of China as this relationship and with Russia within the Soviet Union, so there was no restriction for relations of that kind. "Tomorrow, for example, the province of Banja Luka" - which were the provinces as they were drawn up by Vance and Owen in their plans - "will have relationships with the province of Vojvodina, economic and cultural ones, others. They would sign protocols, exchange various matters and so on. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're focussing on cooperation along those lines. And then I go on to say that "All this can be incorporated into the writing of the constitution." Therefore, it is not something that is being challenged. We're talking about the set-up for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there are no pretensions on that score. I should just like us to take a look at Cosic's intervention. He took the floor and came out in favour strongly of continuing the negotiations and that all that should be done is negotiate, on no account to go to war. And Cosic says, "What we must not do" - on page 55, at the bottom - "is to interrupt our negotiations. I'm afraid, Radovan" - and he's addressing Karadzic - "that as the two of us took part in the negotiations in Geneva that with regard to your proposal, which I agree to, we're excluding ourselves from the Geneva negotiations. This should not happen for the reasons well known to us." And then in the next paragraph he goes to on say, "Therefore, I strive and propose that we hold negotiations at all costs. Negotiations must be held at all cost, which means basically to accept the proposals tabled by them and then to fight for its modification -- their modification." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Cosic's position is quite clear, and his efforts to negotiate, that we must negotiate and negotiate until a solution is ultimately found. Now we come to page 69, and that is the portion that Mr. Nice provided for us in English and extracted from the context of the rest. And I say -- it says "Slobodan Milosevic." "Please, I have to interrupt you. Paspalj said" -- I have to stop you. You've got this, Mr. May, in English. It is the only excerpt from the two minutes, and everything I said in my aspirations for peace. "Paspalj said that we had to have the unity of the Serbian people and de facto we do, because objectively speaking, on all levels, political, military, economic, culture, educational, we have that unity. The problem now is how we could get recognition of this unity, that is, how we could legalise this unity, how we can transform the situation which de facto exists and which could de facto not be threatened, how could we transform it into both de facto and de jure. Therefore, this past, de jure, to get to that, is like --" and then this in inverted commas -- "a small labyrinth." So is that clear that we're referring to negotiations there, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This whole portion relates to negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, re: negotiations. "But, we will never allow a change in this de facto situation, and we will achieve things through the 'labyrinth', if not in half a year, then in a year; if not in a year, then in two. What will we gain? We will gain a decrease in the deaths and therefore preserve our people. Everything must be sacrificed for the people, except the people." Therefore, within the context of everything I said when I took the floor, is this yet another example that negotiations should be continued and that the situation should be solved through negotiations? And then Dobrica Cosic goes on to say that he is in complete agreement, and we continue. And then I go on to say - and these are the most important things for me - the last two words or page 69, that is where this is. "If it says in the first principle constituent people, nation, then we have finished our job." A constituent nation. So that is what we wish to assert and nothing more than that. Isn't that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll do my best to abridge this next portion. Once again, on page 79, there's a brief intervention on my part, once again with regard to the papers. I say, "They complicate matters too much." And I say, "All they have to do is to change it and put in 'constituent nation' and lighten some of the other things and then that is a good basis for you to sit down and prepare the constitution, the long-term preparations for the constitution." And that is what I had to say that time. On page 82, we go back to cooperation between the provinces, and I asked whether the Banja Luka province can have relationships with Vojvodina. Of course it is logical that it can, logical and normal. And that is the response to the question raised by the Prime Minister of the day, Kontic. Is that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says here in the stenographic notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, somebody interjects. I don't remember who Zdravko Zecevic was. He says, "What borders? Borders can only be established through war." Slobodan Milosevic: "No. These borders, with slight adjustments, will be excellent borders. How many -- how much of the percentage of Bosnia-Herzegovina is in these borders? Radovan Karadzic says "40 per cent." Well, this will be increased to 50. There are some 20 that are in dispute at the moment. And Karadzic says, "Posavina and Podrinje are the ones under question." And in Dayton wasn't the agreement 49/51?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that was the solution, in fact, that ratio. And do you remember that Owen said that the war could have ended two years earlier had they had America's support?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, and I also remember that the essential point here was to accept the Vance-Owen Plan, and the fact that there were certain disagreements on certain small -- other points should be negotiated later on and put right, if possible. So the percentage was the same. It would have perhaps been greater with respect to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now take a look at page 95, whereas this fear is expressed again in the following way: Radovan Karadzic says, it's a quotation: "Provinces are not internationally recognised legal entities." He's quoting from the document. "And they cannot enter into agreement with foreign states or international organisations." And then Slobodan Milosevic says, "Of course they're not internationally recognised. The states of America are not internationally recognised legal entities either." And then there's mention of Quebec having 700 agreed conventions with France, and I say, "Well, that is excellent. You'll have as many with Serbia, each province." And this is on page 96. "We have an advantage because Serbia is not an independent state but is within the framework of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, so it will be cooperating also with non-independent states that are part of others." So all these remarks are in the interest of a peaceful solution being found. And then, as during the examination-in-chief, you said that I was the one who negotiated. I don't have my notes exactly how you put it, but that I was the main negotiator with the international community.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the international community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But do you remember that was always upon their request?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said, and that can surely be seen from the notes. The international community insisted on talking to you. So that is nothing terrible about that. It was accepted by the Serbian side. I even remember very well Mr. Holbrooke's speech in the State Department when he said, "Negotiations in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republika Srpska should focus on you and that the other parties should be part of the delegation." And I think that is how it was, and it bore fruit, as we know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My point, Mr. Lilic, is that they insisted upon this and that I endeavoured, as can be seen from these notes, when Yugoslavia was formed that Yugoslavia should take over those things and that we should not interfere. So look at page 112, please. Cosic says to me, "You have an invitation from Vance and Owen" - this is to go to that meeting - "and Momir Bulatovic and me." And Bulatovic says, "Jansen has reiterated that invitation, as he was at the time presiding in the European Community." Cosic says, "We didn't say no to Vance and Owen." Milosevic: "The invitation addressed is up to us. They cannot determine the composition of the Yugoslav delegation. They can give you advice regarding the composition, but that is something quite different. The possibility of going there I am reviewing from one standpoint. Should we, because of his explicit request, accept that invitation?" I'm referring to us from the republics, because I'm advocating that Yugoslavia should be the party negotiating. And when we came before the cameras, he said, "On behalf of the European Community, I have invited President Milosevic to participate in the work of the Geneva conference, to make his contribution," et cetera. I didn't give a response. "We need to think it over. And there is the possibility that if I fail to go, they could say that they are refusing to contribute to the success of the Geneva conference. That is all. That is the whole point." And then Vladislav Jovanovic, who was Foreign Minister at the time, said, "Please review that in a positive light." And on the following page, page 113, this is in the context of the point I'm making that it is the international community that insisted on us making a contribution. It was not us pushing our way in there, but on the contrary, because we thought it was Yugoslavia's duty, that of the federal organs. And on page 113, I say once again, "I will communicate with Vance once again, and if I decide that we shouldn't go, then I will say that a Yugoslav delegation will go without me. I refuse to go three times." Cosic says, "I understand you, and I would refuse it also in your position." Yes, I note the interpreter's remarks that we need to slow down. Slobodan Milosevic said, "We are not a party to the conflict in Bosnia. Serbia is not represented at the conference in Geneva. The Yugoslav delegation is there, and it is the responsibility of the Yugoslav federal institutions. Therefore, we as Yugoslavia are represented." But he insisted, "You cannot refuse to make a contribution." And then I say, "I think it would be a good thing if we resolve the problem in a spirit of understanding, that we should not be stubborn about it," et cetera. Is that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says everything here in this document, and there's no doubt about the fact that your presence there was extremely significant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that is why they requested that I go all the time. I don't know how I come to the next page. Oh, yes, tab 41 now. This is a continuation of the session which was held in several parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. It should be noted for the record that we're dealing with Exhibit 469 and these various tabs come in that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is from this meeting of the council, held also on the 11th of August, and I am suggesting that we send a letter of the following contents. And then I read out a draft of the letter that I wrote. "With reference to the invitation to the 13th Plenary Session of the Conference on Yugoslavia --"

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have tab 41 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is tab 41, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. Lilic doesn't have that tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4, I say that we should send them a reply in response to Carrington's invitation to the 13th Plenary Session in Brussels. And I read, "With reference to the invitation to the 13th Plenary of the Conference on Yugoslavia, I wish to remind you that at the last, 12th, Plenary Session in Brussels, we informed the conference that following the proclamation of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the delegations of the Republics of Serbia and Montenegro in future will be considered a single unified delegation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." And then I say that, "This should be sent to Lord Carrington and signed by Bulatovic and myself," because we had received the invitation. And then Milan Panic, who was at the time already federal Prime Minister, an American of Serb extraction, says, "No one has anything against. No one is opposed. And I propose that the text written by Mr. Milosevic be adopted as written." So we were endeavouring to have Yugoslavia assert itself, and that is what I say on page 10 again. "Our position is that we have done everything we can to create Yugoslavia and for it to survive. We will be talking about the question of state continuity and all other matters." And then I say in the middle of the next paragraph, "Are we going to respect this state that we have formed or not?" So my efforts were directed towards these -- the authorities being -- the authority for this being taken over by the federal institutions. Now, look at page 13 now, please. There's just one remark. I join in when Milan Panic was explaining something, and I say, "The responsibility is with the European Community, which has created the war in Bosnia, and we need to be blamed for it. We need to cover up their crime committed in breaking up an independent state." Panic then says, "But we mustn't say that to him because if you say that, then it's pressing the point and everyone is aware of it anyway." Is that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says here in the stenographic notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on page 10, I say: "If I may add, we should show a maximum respect for the political content of the declaration proclaimed by the Federal Assembly when the constitution was proclaimed. This was achieved through a broad-based democratic process. A platform was established for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I don't see that we need to change the approach taken in the declaration. It is obvious from what we are all saying today that the need is being confirmed of asserting the contents of that very declaration. And I would also add that that declaration has met with a positive response of the international community. It was not met with repulsion or rejection. On the contrary, it was seen as a constructive approach following the formation of Yugoslavia. The world will not start with us around this table. We have a continuity in political behaviour and the platform defined in the declaration." Cosic then says, "I support and confirm this statement." That was our position and I assume you remember that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The declaration was registered in the United Nations too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. This is not directly linked to what we have been saying, but as the situation in Kosovo was referred to, please look at page 88. Slobodan Milosevic: "We have to separate as many Albanians as possible from the separatist movement. The members of the separatist movement and those acting under their pressure will never vote in the elections. Therefore, we must separate the Albanians -- the mass of the Albanians from the separatists. That is the only strategy on which our policies should be based." And then on page 90, in response to what Milan Panic says, "Make him come not because he likes you but make such a situation that he should come." And Milosevic says: "Milan, if they had voted at the elections two years ago today in the People's Assembly of Serbia, they would have 30 members of parliament." I'm referring to the Albanians. "It's not a question of them not being represented. They would be represented indeed, those 30 deputies could have said what they wanted and they could have made draft bills and laws. That is the line of separation, the separatist movement in Kosovo. And I'm not referring to the Albanians as such. The only aim of the separatist movement is to separate Serbia -- Kosovo from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbia and join it to Albania." And then I explain to Panic that, "In spite of the boycott on the elections, we do have several Albanians in parliament from among the ranks of those that did not boycott the elections." So please look at tab 43 very briefly. My criticism of Panic, in connection with the London conference, at which he agreed -- and this is on page 15, page 15. Have you found page 15? At the bottom of the page: Slobodan Milosevic speaking, "That interventions should cease across the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina". "We are not intervening over there. If we had discussed that document, we would have to disprove that." And then he goes on to explain things. I say, "Simply one should write down the truth." That is what is said on page 16. And one can see how many people were sitting round that table at the time. Then there's reference to the assertion of the results of the London conference. Cosic and Panic speak about that. I have not managed last night to read through the entire binder, but I will devote the rest of my time to questions which were left over, had it not been for these binders, that I wanted to address to Mr. Lilic. Mr. Lilic, tell me, please, since you were involved in politics from the beginning, president of the party, president of the Assembly of Serbia, and later president of FRY, vice-premier, et cetera, when did you hear for the first time of the expression "ethnic cleansing"? Was this in connection with the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that if you mean in our country, in the territory of the Republic of Serbia -- because I heard the expression long since in some other situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, as far as I know, at least, it was linked directly to the beginning of terrorist activities, or to be more precise, the beginning of the NATO air raids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember that in Serbia this was an expression used to denote a crime, the worst crime?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when there was reference to this in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, or anywhere else, when ethnic cleansing was referred to --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why I'm asking you whether you meant in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the broader context of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it is certainly linked to the early 1990s, the beginning of the conflict in Bosnia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My precise question is the following: Was this an expression used by us in Serbia to denote a crime, the worst crime?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During all those crises - that is, from the beginning of the conflict in the early 1990s until the end - did the authorities in Serbia and Yugoslavia and I personally seek to protect our entire population, regardless of their ethnicity and on a non-discriminatory basis?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to one of the questions during the last hearing, I said that the ethnic composition of the Republic of Serbia was reminiscent in many ways of the ethnic composition of the former SFRY. Therefore, all those living on the territory of the Republic of Serbia and also the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were given all the necessary care and they were represented in all our legal documents and had -- were able to use those rights. You mentioned a moment ago the failure of the Albanians to utilise their right to vote, which they refused to do. Therefore, throughout the events of the 1990s, Serbia had an almost identical ethnic composition, up until the moment when the Serbs were expelled, upon which the composition changed; there were far more Serbs living in Serbia than before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please: Throughout the time that you spent in political life, which means this whole time coincides with the duration of the conflict, were the Croats and Muslims persecuted during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia in Serbia at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Quite the reverse. And this is easy to prove, not using our own documents but United Nations sources, that thousands of Albanians, yes, and thousands of Muslims crossed into the territory of the Republic of Serbia. There's the case of the brigade, but there are many more drastic cases where people crossed over from Bosnia-Herzegovina to find protection in Serbia. And there are similar examples with members of the Croatian ethnic group. And what I considered to be the highest quality of life living on the territory of the Republic of Serbia is that there were no excesses, no excessive behaviour on an ethnic basis or religious, confessional, national composition. There weren't cases of that kind. Take the example of Vojvodina, for example, which could serve as a standard for Europe as a whole, not only for the Republic of Serbia, Vojvodina province.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the Muslim refugees too. I had information, facts and figures at that time, which I assumed that you as the president of the Serbian assembly are disposed of too. And they told us that we had when the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in that first year, 70.000 Muslim refugees coming in to Serbia from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite correct. I think that actually the figure was far greater later on and 200.000 is the figure mentioned. But this is statistical data. But your figure was quite correct, but as I say, I think there were actually more than 100.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, those people, the Muslims who were fleeing from Bosnia and taking refuge in Serbia, I assume that they did not consider that they were going there to take refuge with the aggressor side. Isn't that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, do you know whether any religious sites were damaged at all -- desecrated at all in Serbia during the duration of these conflicts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, no. According to my information, no, they weren't. I think later on there was a mosque in Novi Pazar which was destroyed, but I think that was during the bombing and that we reconstructed it. I think it has been rebuilt with the participation of the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, let me go on to another matter, something I didn't have a chance to look into because of the short time I had at my disposal. I wasn't able to ask American Ambassador Galbraith, who testified in the meantime between your first testimony here and today. And he presented a report here, dated 1992. August was the month. I don't want to burden you with the report itself. But what I do want to do is to ask you this: I want to ask you this question, and it is entitled "Camps in Serbia." It comes under the heading of "Camps in Serbia." And here is what he writes on page 37, what page 37 of the report says: "A list of concentration camps. [In English] Prisons at the territory -- at the territory of Serbia and Montenegro in which the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina are captive." [Interpretation] And then there are nine enumerated ones in Serbia, two in Montenegro. And I'm going to read out the list. This is what it says: [In English] "Loznica, sport recreation centre." [Interpretation] Sports recreation centre in Loznica, therefore. And the number of detainees, 1.880. And then it says, "Belgrade, the Batajnica airport, 2.200 prisoners there." Then it says, "Belgrade, the barracks, the 4th of July Barracks, 2 and a half thousand detainees." Then Nis comes next, the military centre, military camp, it says, 1 thousand - it's rather small print, so let me have a look, not to make a mistake - 1.540 is the figure there. Then we come to Subotica, and it says, "Assembly point, 5.000 detainees." Then "Aleksinac, closed mine, 4.000 detainees." Sabac is next, 1.440 there. Then Mokra Gora, near Uzice, with 3.000. Then Prijepolje, 480. There you have it. I don't want to go into the second part of that report, but the year is 1992. And this was written -- it was written by, I assume Mr. Galbraith. Yes, it says "Galbraith," and "Michael Miner" the two of them compiled that report. Now, please, is there any truth whatsoever, and could you comment, please, about a piece of information like this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I listened to what you read out carefully, and I'm astounded by what you read out. I don't know where Mr. Galbraith got that data from. I assume that they were people -- if these, all these centres existed at all, that they were people who had fled from the territory of Bosnia and Croatia and happened to be there -- to be listed there. I don't know that concentration camps exist in Serbia, and I think that this is offensive for all the Serb people and for all of us who lived in Serbia, this kind of observation presented by Mr. Galbraith. I say that for this reason: Anybody who knows the history of the Serb people well, and you know full well that we were never a genocidal people, nor did we ever enter into any campaigns and conquests which this is trying to show. Anyway, briefly speaking, I don't know that on the territory of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia there ever existed, not only in 1992, but in all the other years, any camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you would have to have known had they existed; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have had to have known had they existed, especially in these military facilities that are mentioned here. So they are military facilities that you read out, Batajnica, the 4th of July barracks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you happen to remember, in view of the fact that we cooperated closely, that in the beginning several delegations who came to see me on different -- with respect to different questions raised the question about camps in Serbia. And I hope you'll agree -- you'll remember my answer, and that that answer was, "I don't want to convince you of any absurdities. You have a helicopter at your disposal. Fly around. Once you get into the helicopter, put your finger on the map. Go to that place, and see for yourselves whether any camps exist or not." Do you remember me saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that they wanted to convince themselves, to see for themselves, and that you placed these resources at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one delegation went off, and they said, "We'll avail ourselves of your offer," and they went to this mine, this closed mine in Aleksinac; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what they found there was a guard, a watchman, who was a watchman for the whole complex there, looking after the mining equipment, and nobody else. And they did fly out in a helicopter directly to the site to see what they would find. Of course, I offered them this helicopter, and they took me up on the offer. I'm sure you'll remember that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. And I wish to repeat that in Yugoslavia and Serbia throughout that time, almost all the nine years, there were never any incidents on an ethnic basis, on a nationalist basis, nor was there any possibility for setting up anything of the kind. And I think that the public knows, generally speaking, and the press informed us, that even some people that were of different ethnic groups and did commit crimes and were supposed to be prosecuted, we let them off, because we didn't want anybody to think that there were incidents of that kind. We allowed people to go back to Raska without any passports, although Sulejman Ugnjelic [phoen], the case in point, who had left --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was an extremist; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Upon his return from Turkey he was to have been arrested, but allowed him to enter the country and deal in politics, regardless of what was happening behind this political arena, the political stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question, please: With respect to the arming and paramilitary formations, I would just like to remind you, as this was an exhibit here, the minutes from a meeting in 1992 of the Supreme Defence Council. You at the time were not the president, but I'm sure you had a look at the documents. And it is to be found on page 2, last paragraph of point 1, in which it says the following: "Through energetic measures to make individual support to the offices of the Yugoslavian MUP, to prevent all jeopardy to the property, safety of citizens and to prevent any fanning of the flames of national ethnic hostility." And before that, the document stated that, "The state borders towards Bosnia should be controlled, of the -- municipality, and prevent the workings of armed paramilitaries and any other -- and prevent the passage of any armed vehicles that have not been announced." Is it true that when we're talking about paramilitary formations, in general, that those paramilitary formations were organised by individual opposition parties in Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the socialist party ever organise any armed formations of any kind whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I think I said that last time I was here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear from this that it was established that, as it says here, there are -- there was personal support on the part of individual officers of the army and MUP and that efforts were taken to prevent that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And some high-ranking officers of the JNA, as far as I remember it, were replaced and retired. They were pensioned off. And may I just add something, if I may? One more sentence: There was a decision by the Supreme Defence Council from the beginning of 1993 that all paramilitary units should be extinguished, and that kind of order was issued as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did it ever happen that in the leadership of Serbia, in any of the organs and bodies of the leadership, at any position or post, with an open or closed meeting, did anybody ever of our officials, politicians, or at any level - so I'm not limiting you to any level; my level, your level, any level - did they ever strive for an ideal and an idea called Greater Serbia? Did they ever advocate that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, that question or a similar one was one that was raised during my last testimony. And my answer was that it was our position of principle - when I say "ours," the Socialist Party of Serbia - was to preserve Yugoslavia. And many of us joined the party to preserve Yugoslavia. Why? Now, I will repeat the sentence I uttered then: Because that was the only Yugoslavia which was a state in which all Serbs really did live in one country, on the territory they lived in. So I think that was a synonym used by someone else, in fact, where it was our goal, our aim, including my own aim, to preserve the territory occupied by the former Yugoslavia, and all those who wished to leave could leave by peaceful means on the basis of a referendum but the same right should be accorded to people who wished to say, that is to say the Serbs principally, they could stay and live on the territory they had occupied for centuries, so to enjoy the same rights as others. And as far as I am concerned, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whatever it was called later on, that would be the sole real form for having the Serbs live in one state, in a single state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. May I now go on to the next topic. You were the president of the FRY for a full four-year term, the president of the Supreme Defence Council as well. You were in command of the army in wartime and in peace, by virtue of your office as president. Tell me now, please: Did I ever interfere in commanding the army throughout your term of office, throughout your mandate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say again that that was another question you asked me last time, or a similar one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if it was similar, I do apologise, but it's very important. It's an important question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was similar. The fact is, and the rule is, that the president of the Supreme Defence Council is in command of the Army of Yugoslavia in conformity with the decisions taken by the Supreme Defence Council. So I think that the answer is quite clear. The exclusive right is vested in the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did I ever interfere? Did I ever meddle and ask you to make any decisions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing that would go beyond the decisions made by the Supreme Defence Council. If there was any outstanding issue, then the Supreme Defence Council would hold a session, and there were 53 meetings in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the generals or colonels being promoted to rank of general, were they promoted at a request from me at those Supreme Defence Council meetings, following a request from myself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a good answer to that question would be that we dovetailed and coordinated all these positions, with Momir Bulatovic, with you. It was always a concerted effort and they were always good officers, but to satisfy the interests of one and all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is understandable. But can you quote a single example where I had a protege of my own, where I wanted to have somebody promoted or where I wanted to have someone dismissed and replaced perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to remember any case in point to give you a name. Quite certainly - and this is something I said last time - all decisions were arrived at through consensus. So while I was the president of the Supreme Defence Council, there were no outstanding issues with regard to the appointment of generals, promotion of generals or their pensioning off, at least during my term of office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, I would like to ask you just a few more questions which have to do with Resolution 1244, linked to Kosovo. And I'm going to quote some excerpts from that resolution. I have them here. On page 1, the 10th of June, 1999 is the date. Condemning all acts of violence against the Kosovo population as well as all terrorist acts by any party.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation of that. But I have the original text here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Condemning is what it says. It condemns, condemning all acts of violence. And then it goes on to say, "Welcoming the general principles on a political solution [In English] to the Kosovo crisis adopted on 6th of May annexed here to this resolution." [Interpretation] Annex 1: [In English] "And welcoming also the acceptance of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of the principles set forth in points 1 to 9 of the paper presented in Belgrade" [Interpretation] on the 2nd of June, 1999. That is Annex 2 to the resolution, and it says: [In English] "Reaffirming the commitment, all member states --" [Interpretation] the reference is member states of the United Nations -- "to the sovereignty and territorial integrity [In English] of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the other states of the region as set out in the Helsinki final act and Annex 2." [Interpretation] And this is reference to the final act of Helsinki. And then it is said that, "It is decided that a political solution will be based on general principles contained in Annex 1," so the decision is taken to that effect. And then it says in point 3, "Deployment of the international security presence in Kosovo will be synchronised." And then in point 6, it says that, "A special representative will closely coordinate with the international security presence [In English] to ensure that both presence operate towards the same goal and in a mutually supportive manner." [Interpretation] So this is what the resolution says, and I assume you remember that. Then in point 9, under "B" it says: [In English] "The Kosovo Liberation Army and other armed Kosovo Albanian groups, as required in paragraph 15 below." [Interpretation] Now, tell me, please, was the KLA and other groups demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the sovereignty and territorial integrity guaranteed by this resolution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what the resolution says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then under C, point 9, it says, "Establishing a secure environment in which refugees and displaced persons can return home in safety." And then it talks about humanitarian aid to be delivered. And then in D: [In English] "Ensuring public safety and order until the international civil presence can take responsibility for this task." [Interpretation] At the end of point 10, it says, "[In English] To ensure conditions for a peaceful and normal life for all inhabitants of Kosovo." [Interpretation] So that was the obligation taken upon itself by the international forces, the conditions for a peaceful and a normal life of all the citizens of Kosovo. Is it true that that was not achieved or fulfilled but that, rather, under the auspices of the United Nations, more than 250.000 Serbs were expelled from Kosovo after the forces arrived, which according to this resolution, were meant to protect everyone? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What the Resolution 1244 says is correct. De jure, that is what it was. But the de facto situation in Kosovo was quite different. Not only were 250.000 people expelled, but last time I mentioned something which I would like to repeat. It is a fact that Pristina there are only 200 Serbs remaining. There were more than 40.000 before. They are all living in one apartment block. And after the last act signed by Mr. Steiner, I think it will be hard for anyone to return to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let us clear this up. The international community pledged that it would create conditions for a peaceful and normal life for all the inhabitants of Kosovo, whereas under its auspices, 350.000 people were expelled of which 250.000 were Serbs and 100.000 other non-Albanians. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And about another 300.000 Albanians have resettled there, have settled there, coming from different European countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is correct. It says in point 15: [In English] "The KLA and other armed Kosovo Albanian groups end immediately all offensive actions and comply with the requirement for demilitarisation as laid down by the head of international security presence in consultation with a special representative of the Secretary-General." [Interpretation] That hasn't been done either, has it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, none of that is in dispute. Only I think we differ on one point. I think you and I could have done all that before the international community arrived. We could have made a census of the population. You know that I even asked you and spoke to His Holiness, the Patriarch of Serbia, Mr. Pavle, to see what is the church property in Kosovo and Metohija. I think we would have been much more effective. What you are saying is quite correct, but I think the Serbs have nothing -- gained nothing from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is: Is it true that they did not fulfil what they promised through this resolution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under J it even says, "Protecting and promoting human rights." What human rights of Serbs can be even referred to over there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no Serbs there. And of course the very few that are left have no rights at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it says that it decides that an international civil and security presence are established -- [In English] Are established for an initial period of 12 months, to continue thereafter unless the Security Council decides otherwise." [Interpretation] And then there's Annex 1, in which there's reference again to demilitarisation of the terrorist organisation the KLA. Then there's Annex 2, which in point 5 again says: [In English] " -- a normal life for all inhabitants in Kosovo." [Interpretation] And then in point 6 it says, of this Annex 2: "After withdrawal a agreed number of Yugoslav and Serbian personnel will be permitted to return [In English] To perform the following functions: Liaison with the international civil mission and the international security presence, making clearing minefields, maintaining a presence at Serb patrimonial sites, maintaining a presence at key border crossings." [Interpretation] Therefore, all these things envisaged by the UN resolution has not been fulfilled; isn't that right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Neither the military nor the military personnel were not allowed to return and we have a situation of occupation rather than the situation proclaimed by this UN resolution. And again, in point 8 of this Annex 2, it says -- it refers to the principle of sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. And again, the demilitarisation of the KLA and again negotiations between the two parties. None of this was carried out; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I said, as far as the sovereignty over Kosovo and Metohija is concerned, that is, the sovereignty of the Republic of Serbia over that area, there's not the letter "S" left of sovereignty, even though it is prescribed by the resolution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that even when this UN resolution has been trampled upon what would have happened with any other kind of agreement that doesn't have that weight? Is there any higher authority than the UN?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, I should like to remind you, for the reasons that you confirmed a moment ago, of just a part of a speech at a congress. I will not quote from the one I've already quoted from for these reasons - and I say: "This shameful mission of the so-called international community in Kosmet, which has experienced a fiasco in every respect should be brought to an end as soon as possible and that the authorities of our country should take over full competence over our own territory. Unlike them, we are quite capable, without anyone's assistance, to ensure peace and security for all citizens on a footing of equality." And then - and I hope you will remember this, but that transcript was served on us by the opposing side - I say that "Despite all the blows that Serbia has received from the world through sanctions and turning a deaf eye to the suffering of a small and peace-loving people, to the expectations that things, over the evil hovering above it, will be resolved of its own, in some miraculous way, that the tyrants will get tired of choking one and the same victim and look around for another one somewhere. "So despite all those blows, Serbia and we over here do not wish anyone ill. We would not like to retaliate for this bloody payback, this bloody debt. We are still inclined to act in a Christian or leftist way - who knows which - and to believe in the victory of good and justice, but our experience, as well as the experience of other nations, has taught us that good and justice do not come of their own accord, that enormous and, with time, organised efforts are required to defeat evil, hatred, and violence among peoples." Do you remember that, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a speech delivered at a congress, at our congress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And do you recall, as at the time you were still the vice-premier, apart from all the things that are not in dispute from the UN resolution, as the fact that none of it was fulfilled is not in dispute, that the day Ahtisaari and Chernomyrdin came to Belgrade a meeting was held, a plenary meeting, of a Yugoslav and Russian delegation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a meeting, but I really don't know the composition of the participants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that can easily be verified. Everyone was present. Milan Milutinovic, the president of the Serbia, Zivadin Jovanovic, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, some other officials who participated --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was nowhere near being involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But our generals attended the meeting as well. In fact, there were too many people present at that meeting for anything to be presented falsely, and there was Chernomyrdin heading the Russian delegation and Russian generals. I'm sure you remember the report about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know General Ivasa [phoen] well from that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were there. Did you know that Chernomyrdin, on behalf of President Yeltsin and on behalf of Russia, formally guaranteed that Russia would not agree to a resolution being adopted on the basis of chapter 7 and if such a resolution is adopted pursuant to chapter 7, Russia would veto it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even this resolution was, after all, adopted pursuant to chapter 7, and even as such it was not respected. The only question is who is to blame for this, Chernomyrdin or the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, this is a very long way from what the witness can give evidence about. And your time is now up. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes. And then the amicus when we come back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just finish my last question? You interrupted me as I was halfway through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It was not a matter which the witness could deal with. He wasn't at the meeting. All he could say was he'd read a report about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you didn't let me finish the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I know I didn't, because it wasn't something he could deal with. It was well away from his time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I finish my question, you will see that he's able to answer it. It will only take 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll see if he can. But less than 30 seconds. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less than 30 seconds. I promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, I'm not talking about the Russian delegation, which certainly was acting in good faith, but I'm talking about violence that was applied to us and them and the UN in the crime committed against our people. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, you've got half an hour, up to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honours, to finish even before then, but I will simply not have time to refer to the documents we received in the last two days, even though there would be many questions to be asked. But I would like to ask Mr. Lilic if he could tell me in general terms, if he could look at that big binder and say that in the tabs from 35 to 39 mainly contain decisions of the military authorities during the period when he was Supreme Commander. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could just look through them very quickly because I have very little time. So I'm talking about tabs 35 to 39. Those were decisions taken by the military authorities at a time when you were the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia. From 35 to 39. Just look quickly at the dates, please. They are decisions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this for the first time too, so I'm afraid I can't answer so quickly. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should just like to draw your attention, Your Honours, to this. You can check this. These were decisions taken during the period -- during the term of office of Mr. Lilic as president of the state. I would also like to draw your attention to something which I consider to be of significance; that all the tabs from 40 through to the end were compiled when the president of the country was Dobrica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what I would like to ask you, Mr. Lilic, if you can give me a brief answer - I won't be suggestive at all or leading - do you know what happened in Hrcovci [phoen] in Vojvodina, at a point in time in the initial period of all these events in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know stories about it linked to the Croats living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That was the incident I'm referring to. Could you explain to Their Honours what happened and what the authorities in Serbia undertook in that connection.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me with any certainty to comment on that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I won't insist. But then when you were asked about camps that may have existed in the territory of Serbia, do you remember that immediately after Vukovar a number of captured Croatian citizens were in Sremska Mitrovica and at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the only case you know of that people from another republic were in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, and do you know that later on they were more or less all exchanged for captured Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were the Supreme Commander of the Army of Yugoslavia for four years as the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, from 1993 to 1997, so for exactly half of the crisis period of 1991 to 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was president of the Supreme Defence Council for four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia, which you were the Supreme Commander, ex officio, came into being in 1992, after Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia were internationally recognised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I explained that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you did say that. I will ask you something else in that connection. In terms of personnel and materiel, it came into existence, it emerged out of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during conflicts in the territory of the ex-Yugoslavia already in June -- no, no, but let me -- I apologise. Let me ask you something else first. Is it true that the Territorial Defences in the republics up until June 1992 were under the command of the JNA and that both the weapons and the equipment were the property of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that connection, is it true that the Territorial Defence of Slovenia already in June grew into a Slovenian army and that, in terms of personnel and materiel, it was formed out of the personnel and equipment of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. And the identical situation applied in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But the first army that developed out of the former JNA was the Slovenian army. And the Supreme Commander was Mr. Milan Kucan as the president of the Republic of Slovenia. I didn't have time to ask him that question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many men the Army of Yugoslavia numbered at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the precise figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the same happened in Croatia. I don't have to go into that with you. Is it true that the Army of Yugoslavia -- that no fire was opened at in Macedonia, that it withdrew without firing a single shot?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you: The Yugoslav People's Army, not the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is the only place where fire was not opened against the JNA and the JNA withdrew without a single shot being fired.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next thing I'd like to ask you to explain to Their Honours has to do with the relationship between the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as the Supreme Commander, towards the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, as you were the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody else, except for you, who was Supreme Commander -- who was able to issue any kind of order, oral or in writing, to the general staff or, rather, the chief of the general staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the Army of Yugoslavia, in conformity with the Supreme Defence Council's decisions, and president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was at the head, so nobody could issue a written or oral order to the chief of the general staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the best example for that - and here I have to go back to tab 19 of 469, Exhibit 469, an example quoted here - where General Momcilo Perisic, as the chief of the general staff, addresses you, and he writes a letter to you in which he states that he has received a request from the president of the republic with respect to some volunteers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And your answer was - and this is also in that same tab - you issued an order of the 29th of September, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is what you say in that order: "We prohibit reception and training in the Army of Yugoslavia of all persons, including volunteers," under point 1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And under point 2, "Reception and training from -- the reception and training of the persons from item 1 of this order, in the Yugoslav army, can be carried out only with my approval, given on the basis of the Supreme Defence Council"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that the principle which was used in the relationship between the general staff and the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only principle that met with the law and the command of the Yugoslav army with respect to singleness of command and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that how it was between the 15th of June, 1992 and the 1st of June, 1995, when the president of Yugoslavia was Dobrica Cosic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it should have been. It's difficult for me to answer whether it actually was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But that was the principle.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the same thing true while the presidency of the SFRY was still in existence? But let me not dwell on that. There was a sole member examined here, Mr. Stipe Mesic, who was a member of the Yugoslav State Presidency. He testified here. But at that time too, did this principle hold true that orders to the general staff and to General Kadijevic could have been issued only --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the president of the Yugoslav state presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean as the collective presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as the collective Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Now could you please be given tab 20 of 469. And this brings us to the point where you yourself were the participant in the decision-making process and the signing of the agreement. I'm referring to a meeting by the representatives of the top leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska, which was held on the 29th of August, 1995 in Dobanovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We already discussed the matter here. The Court has heard about it at length. But I'd like to dwell on one particular fragment which I feel to be significant for Their Honours's decision-making process later on. You see at the end that mention is made of the fact that the meeting was attended by the Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Mr. Pavle, and Bishop Irinej Bulovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you take a look at page 7. There we have what the Bishop Irinej said. And this is what he said: "We must, however, accept the clear fact that the international community will not negotiate with the leaders of Republika Srpska but with President Milosevic. But President Milosevic will not negotiate alone, himself, but wishes to include into the delegation representatives of Republika Srpska too." Do you remember that, that that was said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you to take a look at page 12 -- page 12, when the Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church asked to be given the floor and he said the following: "It is much more important what is being signed rather than who is doing the signing." And he repeated the church's appeal to agreement, unity. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the agreement had already been prepared for signing and when you were all due to sign, as it says here on page 15, everything was already prepared and ready for signing, and when it came to the signing of the document offered up, the leadership of Republika Srpska demanded that the assembly at Pale state their views. And this was taken has an attempt of the united approach before the international community to be put off indefinitely. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had already had some bad experience with that kind of behaviour, and that is why we insisted upon having it signed straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at one point there was the danger of complete divergence between the two leaderships. And Patriarch Pavle cautioned that he would not leave the room until there was agreement and unity on the part of the Serbian leaders and that they would -- he could only be taken out by force, and he hoped that that wouldn't be the case. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And may I just add in quotation marks that our side, meaning the FRY side, signed the document without the signature of the representatives of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But President Karadzic asked for a new break, a pause, and it was only after that break that the document was signed. So was the Patriarch's influence the overruling one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. He prevailed upon the leadership of Republika Srpska. So his presence was the decisive -- it was very important. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you one more thing: Today we looked at transcripts or, rather, exhibits linked to the telephone conversations. Now, from all this, does the following emerge, what we heard from you today, that neither you nor Perisic nor the president of Serbia were able to issue orders to the leadership of Republika Srpska about any matter at all? Is that -- would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we take into account all the peace plans that fell through because of, if I can use the word, their understanding of the case, then we could draw that conclusion the way you put it just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to the last part of my questioning. And in order to do so, I'd like you to have tab 3 in front of you, tabs 3 and 4, although I'm not going to dwell on tab 4 for any length of time. It is Exhibit 469 once again. You responded to questions asked in the examination-in-chief, although you weren't asked a lot. Several extracts from this document. It is a programme, a party programme, a programme of the party to which you belonged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Your Honours, on page 10 of that document, last paragraph of the English translation, says the following:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That your party considers, believes, that the autonomous provinces in Serbia cannot be states but can only be a form of territorial autonomy for which the constitution establishes and guarantees the autonomous rights which saw an expression of the specific national, historic, and cultural specificities of the regions in question. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does that mean, to all intents and purposes, that in keeping with that programme that the amendments to the constitution of the Republic of Serbia took place, which in practical terms means that the sole thing that was abolished was the right to use the veto, the right of veto which existed within Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to be quite clear. This attribute of state-hood was abolished. All the other rights remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And up until that point in time, Serbia was not able to have a united front towards the rest of the country, and within the republic everybody could use the right of veto. And Serbia was not able to have any question prevail which was of general importance for all the people in Serbia. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you remember - and you were a businessman at the time, but as of 1990 you were a politician - do you happen to recall that this right of veto was most often used when the budget was determined for the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know that. Right. If you don't know that, do you know this, that the right of veto was used very frequently at a point in time where decisions were called upon to be made with regard to assistance to the underdeveloped areas?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to dwell on former times, but in 1990 in particular the right of veto was used by Slovenia and Croatia with respect to that issue, and that there were areas that previously could always count on receiving aid and assistance and that it was representatives from Croatia and Slovenia that started to curtail that right. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there is evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to dwell on something else with respect to this document, and that is page 11, paragraph 5 of the chapter on national equality and federalism, in the English version, page 11, national equality and federalism; and the B/C/S version is on page 10. And this is what it says: "With the new Yugoslav constitution, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in existence, the new Yugoslav constitution allow for the forming of Autonomous Provinces in Yugoslavia --" isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all that was discussed, exclusively that question. And that is what it says in this second programme too. As to the other parts where the Serbs lived, all it says is that they should continue to receive aid and assistance as had previously been done in the times when the country helped its underdeveloped regions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I still have another few points with respect to Kosovo to clear up, looking at the period when you yourself were president, of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is. Now, do you know about this, are you aware of this as a generally known fact, and it relates to events taking place between the 1980s and 1990s, although you weren't a politician at the time: But do you know that the demands for a republic, Kosovo Republic, and independence in Kosovo, began as early on as 1981? There were armed conflicts that broke out, and this question was always supported from some other parts of Yugoslavia too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of the fact that during that period of time another thing that happened was this,: Very often the Serbs left Kosovo but there were a lot of emigrants from Albania coming in at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are they figures that are quite substantial?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A large number of Albanians coming into the area were -- received assignments. And there are precise data that the JNA has that they were secret agents and that they had their agendas to populate Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this during the terrorist actions that took place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at the time after 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying to get through as much material as possible in the time I have, but I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
